01 / SUCCESS

Reach the target in budget.

The true object center must finish within 5.5 cm of the target without crossing the table limit. Every attempt counts, up to seven moves.

02 / COST

Pay for each interaction.

Time includes pushing, settling, and an assumed 0.6-second setup per move. Computation and real robot travel are not included.

03 / VALIDITY

Simulation is one level of evidence.

The browser and contact solver use different dynamics implementations. Both are virtual. Field performance needs real measurements.

USEFUL DATA

Measure both phases.

Record from rest, through the force pulse, and after release. Use varied forces and durations. Quiet or nearly identical motion may not separate mass from friction.

HONEST VALIDATION

Hold out whole trials.

Do not split neighboring frames from the same push across both groups. Keep a final test set if you use validation results to choose changes to the model.

WHAT A PASS MEANS

Better prediction on this data.

Lower held-out error supports this model for these conditions. It does not prove robot policy transfer, hardware reliability, or deployment readiness.

METHOD / TASK-SPECIFIC WORLD MODEL

A model that can change its mind.

Predict a physical outcome, compare it with motion, and revise the belief.

01

Observe

Read noisy XY positions before the push, at force release, and after settling.

02

Predict

Test force pulses against 247 possible friction and mass pairs.

03

Choose

Balance target error, table-limit risk, time, and an optional information bonus.

04

Update

Use motion measurements to change the probability of each physics pair.

WHAT IS LEARNED

Two physical parameters.

Friction and object mass are unknown. The starting model is a probability distribution. The model structure, gravity, commanded motor force, and pusher mass are known.

During contact, the force accelerates the object and the light pusher. After release, the object slows under friction. Observing both phases helps distinguish friction from mass.

HOW ACTIONS ARE CHOSEN

A small search, every move.

All strategies search the same bounded force pulses toward the target. Fixed keeps its starting belief. Passive updates after task moves. Active also rewards an approximate information score.

A learning move is an action Active selects over its task-only choice. It can also make progress. This is a heuristic, with a one-move planning horizon.

WHEN THE MODEL IS WRONG

Confidence needs checking.

The likelihood includes measurement covariance and a model-error allowance. A large unexpected residual reopens the parameter range.

That rule can miss failures. The 90% ranges are model-based, and the table-limit penalty does not provide a physical safety guarantee.

IDEAL RADIAL CONTACT / SI UNITS

a = max(0, (F − μmg) / (m + mₚ))
d_push = ½ aT²
d_coast = (aT)² / (2μg)

F: motor force · T: pulse time · m: object mass
mₚ: pusher mass (0.06 kg) · μ: friction

What the independent solver adds

MuJoCo has a gravity-supported object, a table, and a separate pusher with two force-driven joints. Object movement comes from pusher contact. No horizontal launch velocity or direct object force is injected.

The pusher retracts after each pulse and is repositioned for the next move. The round object can translate in two dimensions; rotation is locked. The browser uses an ideal contact approximation.

WHY THIS COULD MATTER

Less retuning for new objects.

The product hypothesis is a physics adaptation module for robot teams. It could help a planner adjust when object weight or surface conditions change. Benefits need hardware and customer validation.

WHAT COMES NEXT

Check against real motion.

Collect measured force and object tracks, check held-out prediction errors, then test whether simulated action choices transfer. Add rotation and more complex contacts only with separate validation.

RELATED WORK

Build on existing research.

Phys2Real studies online physical adaptation. SIMPLER studies useful simulated evaluations. This project is a small engineering study, with explicit baselines and probe costs.
